title: Protecting Norway’s Gas From Russia
content:
In any direct confrontation, European critical infrastructure would almost certainly become a target of the Kremlin’s long-range strikes, as it sought to degrade the continent’s warfighting capacity and population’s will to resist. 

One underappreciated vulnerability in Europe’s economic system is Norway’s natural gas infrastructure. Since 2022, Norway has replaced Russia as the continent’s main supplier, delivering 89 billion cubic meters to the European Union in 2025, almost one-third of the bloc’s gas imports and more than half of its pipeline supply. 

Russia’s share of EU gas continues to decline, while geopolitical volatility is making several other non-EU suppliers, foremost the US, less attractive. Norway’s role can be expected to grow further, both in its share of supply and political weight. 

Dependence on Norwegian gas is particularly high in Germany, the continent’s industrial powerhouse, whose factories are critical to European rearmament. In 2025, Norway supplied 44% of German gas imports, and industrial customers accounted for 60% of German gas consumption.

title: Europe and China 3 – The Coming Showdown
content:
This is the third of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe. 

The negative numbers began to cascade across European balance sheets as soon as China entered the World Trade Organization in late 2001.  

But the cost-benefit calculations were not equal for all Europeans. Some nations, such as Germany, initially gained from high-value exports and joint ventures. Others, like Greece and Portugal, faced a surge of low-cost Chinese goods and strategic investments by entities linked to the Chinese state. 

The Chinese economy was barely one-eighth the size of that of the European Economic Community before the People’s Republic embarked on its policy of “reform and opening up” at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee in December 1978. By 2025, the relative economic weight of China and the European Union was almost equal.  

Together they account for about a third of world trade. In 1975, their bilateral trade was worth about €2bn ($2.2bn) annually; 50 years later, it was €2bn a day, according to figures compiled for the Institut Jacques Delors.
snippet: This is the third of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe.
creator: Kinsey Burr

title: Europe and China 2 – The Age of Developing Disillusion
content:
This is the second of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe.

At first, necessity was the mother of partnership between European commerce and the People’s Republic of China. At Swiss business schools, the example of Schindler, the elevator maker, remains a keynote study.

In 1979, the Swiss company became an early joint venture partner with China, even though it had ties with Jardine Matheson, the Hong Kong-based trading house associated with the opium trade of the 19th century. The reason: China had a housing crisis. It was expanding skyward because a growing population required tower blocks.

The country lacked sophisticated technology and had to shop abroad. Eventually, the Swiss firm won out over Japanese and American competitors. Politics played a part. Switzerland had recognized the People’s Republic in 1950, and it was a neutral power. Today China has a giant domestic elevator industry of its own plus joint ventures with, among others, Kone of Finland and Hitachi of Japan.
snippet: This is the second of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe.
creator: Sara George

title: New US Chip Controls Squeeze Europe
content:
What does the Jensen Huang Megaspeed scandal mean for Europe? At first glance, not much: Europeans will keep buying Nvidia chips. But a closer look shows that the ripple effects will have consequences for transatlantic relations and for Europe’s increasingly tense relationship with Beijing. The Netherlands and its star chip machine manufacturer, ASML, look particularly vulnerable.

Huang was perhaps Washington’s most influential China dove. He almost single-handedly persuaded President Donald Trump and his cabinet to take a lax approach to enforcing Biden-era export controls on Nvidia chips, to the fury of hawks on both sides of the aisle. His diminished influence, coupled with fresh revelations around the extent of illegal chip smuggling to China via Singapore, means that the hawks once again have the wind in their sails.  

The Department of Commerce has already moved to block Chinese AI companies from using overseas data centers. Three bills look set to be rolled into the National Defense Authorization Act that would further crack down on China’s use of US chips.

title: Europe and China 1 – The Arrival of the People’s Republic
content:
This is the first of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe.

In the 1990s, the shadow of Tiananmen Square fell across Europe’s trade relations with China. The massacre of protesters in 1989 marked a return to dictatorship and wiped out hopes of political reform. European firms drew back, an arms embargo was imposed, and political pressure grew to isolate “the butchers of Beijing.”

Yet by the end of the decade China had swept triumphantly into the World Trade Organisation (WTO), its economy was growing fast, and the world was at its door as a new word, “globalization,” set the agenda at every corporate summit.

To reconstruct the turnaround, a historian must first identify the political personalities behind it. Even as the blood was hosed off Tiananmen — and while the future President Xi Jinping’s wife, the singer Peng Liyuan, serenaded the martial law troops — many Chinese leaders knew they had made a terrible blunder.

They included Xi Jinping’s father, the twice-purged army veteran Xi Zhongxun, who paid homage in public to the “wise” and “resolute” decision to suppress “a counter-revolutionary riot” but in private mourned the setback to economic reform.
snippet: This is the first of a three-part series on China’s relationship with Europe.
creator: Sara George

title: Starlink Squeeze: Europe Searches for Alternatives
content:
For the second time in recent weeks, Starlink restrictions disrupted Ukrainian military operations, reinforcing Europe’s urgency to reduce its dependence on the US satellite service. In response, the continent is racing to catch up in the space satellite race, even if wholesale battlefield replacement remains a long-term goal.

Due to the disruption, Ukrainian drones faced speed limits of about 161 kilometers per hour, far below the normal 400-kilometer-per-hour limits. Responsibility remains disputed, though the slowdown coincided with US mediators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff’s visit to Moscow.

Europe’s efforts to find alternatives to the on-again, off-again Starlink service are gaining speed. GOVSATCOM, operational since January, pools existing European national satellite capacity. Eutelsat’s OneWeb serves Ukraine with its 600 low-Earth-orbit satellites. Its terminal range is improving. Intellian’s military manpack, introduced early this year, supports GPS-denied operation when paired with approved positioning equipment.

title: Ukraine’s Army Has Grown Up
content:
The Ukrainian Armed Forces launched a major organizational reform early in 2025, introducing a corps-based structure. The aim was to establish larger operational formations that bring brigades, artillery, drone units, logistics, and intelligence under a single command.  

Those changes are now bearing fruit as battlefield commanders are encouraged to make their own decisions and cast aside the Russian legacy of reference to faraway senior officers. 

Each corps, operating with greater autonomy, would be responsible for a specified sector of the front. The new structure was designed to improve coordination along a front line stretching more than 1,000km (620 miles), while accelerating decision-making on the battlefield.  

The shift away from a Soviet-style, top-down system toward a more decentralized approach has accelerated significantly since General Mykhailo Drapatyi became commander-in-chief in July. He is bringing much-needed change to the military’s culture.

title: The Nvidia Scandal Exposes American Blind Spots
content:
Washington has built an elaborate web of export controls and licensing requirements to keep artificial intelligence chips from reaching China.

Yet Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s apparent “honeytrap” affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of passing information to Beijing, is about more than the blind spots of those controls. It is about the difficulty of shutting down access to advanced tech in a globalized, interconnected world — and about a company, a regulator, and an executive branch that saw warning signs and were slow act on them. 

Had existing rules been enforced, Nvidia should never have been selling advanced chips to the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International. Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, which became a major Nvidia customer, and attracted scrutiny over possible violations of American export controls. Nvidia’s board has retained outside counsel to investigate whether Chinese intelligence targeted their former CEO, who resigned after his affairs were revealed. The company maintains that it has no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised.
snippet: Washington has built an elaborate web of export controls and licensing requirements to keep artificial intelligence chips from reaching China.
creator: Jack Galloway

title: Survival in Ukraine’s Fortress Cities
content:
Driving around Kramatorsk, Sarah Ashton, Senior Sergeant of the 46th Brigade, points out what has been recently destroyed, what was hit months ago, and which businesses are still open. She also has a growing list of places she no longer wants to go.

Damaged bridges, demolished buildings, burned cars and stores whose names now serve as reference points for attacks accompany her journeys. Stopping for something to eat means leaving the vehicle outside and hoping it will still be intact when she returns.

An American serving in Ukrainian military intelligence, Sarah drives me through fortress-belt cities of Kramatorsk and neighboring Sloviansk. The cities are key to Vladimir Putin’s aim of capturing the Donbas, which comprises the oblasts of Luhansk and Donetsk in eastern Ukraine. He has now asked US mediators to persuade Kyiv to surrender this land, and it’s fair to describe this as No. 1 on the Kremlin’s list of demands.

A sliver of Luhansk and some 25% of Donetsk is still in government hands, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, two of its biggest cities. They used to each have a population of a couple of hundred thousand. Not anymore.

title: Putin’s Propagandists Promise the Peace of the Graveyard
content:
The outcome of the midterm elections in the United States filled the studios of the Russian state media outlets with unadulterated sorrow.   

During his radio show Full Contact on November 4, state TV host Vladimir Solovyov grimly surmised, “Trumpushka failed.” Appearing on the state TV program Sunday Evening With Vladimir Solovyov last week, the head of RT Margarita Simonyan dramatically exclaimed that US President Donald Trump was America’s last hope.  

In reality, it seems to be the Kremlin’s last hope of achieving Ukraine’s unconditional capitulation by severing US support. The US still sells weapons to Ukraine and provides intelligence, although military and financial aid was largely terminated in early 2025, and Starlink satellite services continue to be limited, 

But Moscow wants much more. Pundits and experts explicitly say that they aim to reach and influence the American president, believing their words on state media are conveyed to Trump by the US Embassy in Russia.
snippet: The outcome of the midterm elections in the United States filled the studios of the Russian state media outlets with unadulterated sorrow.
